sentences.text: Dromaeosauroides bornholmensis is the only species in a genus of dromaeosaurid dinosaur, a group of carnivorous theropods.
The genus name translates to "Dromaeosaurus-like," while the species name indicates its origin from the island of Bornholm.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — consists of a single tooth crown measuring 21.7 mm in length, 9.7 mm in width, and 6.6 mm at the base.
This tooth is curved and finely serrated, featuring six square, chiseled denticles per millimeter along its cutting edges.
Dromaeosauroides holds the distinction of being the first and only scientifically named dinosaur known from Denmark.
It is recognized as one of the oldest known dromaeosaurs and the first uncontested dromaeosaur from the Early Cretaceous of Europe.
The holotype tooth was officially certified as "Danekræ," meaning "Danish creature," to highlight its scientific importance.
A second known tooth was later found, measuring 15 mm in length with features identical to the holotype.
The genus was named by Christiansen and Bonde in 2003 based on remains discovered in the Jydegaard Formation on the island of Bornholm.
The first remains were two teeth found in 2000 and 2008, with the initial tooth discovered during a field course taught by Christiansen and Bonde in September 2000.
A geology student named Eliza Jarl Estrup found the first dinosaur tooth on Danish territory during that specific field course.

Estimates of the animal's size vary; one assessment places it at approximately 2 to 3 meters long and weighing about 40 kg, while another suggests a body length of 3 meters or more, possibly reaching 4 meters.
Flight was considered unlikely for an animal of this size, despite some smaller dromaeosaurs potentially being capable of flight.
Studies suggest dromaeosaurs used their sickle claws to grasp prey while dismembering them with their mouths, similar to how modern birds of prey grip and pin down prey.
Milàn and colleagues speculated that it could have used its enlarged sickle claw for "spear fishing" to catch fish like Lepidotes, based on coprolite evidence.
The development of deep snouts in dromaeosaurids was likely an adaptation for handling vertebrate prey.

In 2003, Christiansen and Bonde classified it as a member of the Dromaeosaurinae subfamily within Dromaeosauridae due to similarities with Dromaeosaurus, though it is not considered part of that genus because the two lived 60 million years apart.
Dromaeosauroides lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically within the Berriasian age between 139.1 and 137.05 million years ago.
It inhabited a coastal lagoon environment alongside sauropods.
Remains of the Scandinavian-Russian Early Cretaceous fauna, including Dromaeosauroides, are found only in Bornholm and Scania.

In 2008, Johan Lindgren and colleagues considered it an indeterminate dromaeosaur, while in 2010, Oliver W. M. Rauhut and colleagues suggested that similar teeth might belong to the tyrannosauroid Proceratosaurus rather than Dromaeosauroides. In 2021, Nicholas R. Longrich and colleagues proposed that it may have been an early eudromaeosaur.
